stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
After Harlow County required chain restaurants to post calorie counts on their menus, health researchers compared sales receipts from the year before the rule with those from the year after. The average number of calories per transaction fell by 6 percent. The researchers concluded that seeing the numbers had led diners to order lower-calorie items.

Text 2
The Harlow County receipts do show a real decline. But many chains did not want to print four-digit numbers next to their signature dishes, so in the months before the rule began they quietly shrank portions and changed recipes. Diners could have ordered exactly what they always had and still taken in fewer calories.
choices: The labeling requirement helped reduce the calories in a typical restaurant purchase in Harlow County.
Once calorie counts appeared on menus, Harlow County diners began choosing lower-calorie items.
Changes to portions and recipes, not diners' choices, account for the entire drop in calories.
A 6 percent drop in calories per transaction is too small to make a difference to public health.
explanation: Write the two sentences first. Author 1 thinks the labels lowered calories because diners changed what they ordered. Author 2 thinks the drop is real but could have come from restaurants changing the food. Now look at why the chains changed their recipes: they didn't want to post large numbers once the rule took effect. So in Author 2's account the rule still causes the decline, just through a different mechanism. Both authors therefore accept that the labeling requirement helped lower the calories in a typical purchase. They disagree about how it did so, and choice A doesn't take a side on that.

B.why: This is Text 1's conclusion, the exact claim Text 2 was written to doubt. Text 2 says diners 'could have ordered exactly what they always had.' You probably noticed that the two texts share a lot and assumed they share the conclusion as well.

C.why: Text 2 only says reformulation 'could have' produced the drop. That casts doubt on Text 1's explanation without proving a different one. Author 1 would reject this statement, and Author 2 never goes this far. You went from 'not established' to 'the opposite is proven.'

D.why: Neither author questions whether 6 percent matters. Text 2 even calls the decline 'real.' The texts disagree about what caused the drop, not how big it was, so this choice is about something neither author discusses.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Seismologist Rafael Ortiz examined forty years of records from the Calder Fault. He found that each of the fault's four magnitude 6 earthquakes was preceded, within a month, by a swarm of dozens of small tremors. Ortiz therefore concluded that such swarms can serve as warnings that a major earthquake is approaching.

Text 2
Ortiz is right that no major Calder earthquake has arrived without a swarm first. Yet the same records contain more than thirty comparable swarms that ended quietly. A swarm, then, says little about whether a major earthquake is coming, since nearly every swarm on the fault has been followed by nothing larger.
choices: During the period Ortiz studied, every major Calder Fault earthquake came after a swarm of small tremors.
When a swarm of small tremors strikes the Calder Fault, a major earthquake is likely to follow soon.
Swarms of small tremors have had no connection to the major earthquakes on the Calder Fault.
Forty years of records are too few to show whether swarms come before major Calder earthquakes.
explanation: Author 1 thinks that swarms came before every major quake, so swarms can serve as warnings. Author 2 begins by granting the first half ('no major Calder earthquake has arrived without a swarm first') and then rejects the conclusion: most swarms are followed by nothing larger. The concession is the point they share. Notice which way it runs. 'Every major quake had a swarm before it' is a different claim from 'a swarm means a major quake is coming.' Both authors accept the first, which is choice A.

B.why: This is the trap that remains after you have spotted the shared ground. You saw that both authors link swarms and major quakes, then read the link in the wrong direction. 'Swarms predict quakes' is Ortiz's conclusion, and Text 2 rejects it because more than thirty swarms 'ended quietly.'

C.why: Text 2 accepts that every major quake was preceded by a swarm, which is a real connection. It only denies that a swarm reliably signals a quake. You treated Author 2's narrower doubt as a complete rejection of any link.

D.why: Neither author questions the record. Text 2 relies on 'the same records' to make its own argument. You assumed Author 2 must be attacking the evidence when Author 2 is actually attacking the inference drawn from it.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Engineer Tamsin Okafor mixed dormant bacterial spores into concrete. When the hardened samples were cracked and kept damp, the bacteria revived and deposited limestone, sealing fissures up to 0.4 millimeters wide within a month. Okafor concluded that the additive will substantially extend the service life of highway bridges.

Text 2
Okafor's samples did seal themselves. But they sat indoors at a steady 20°C, wet throughout. Bridge decks freeze, dry out for weeks, and are salted each winter, and no one has tested whether the spores survive years inside such a slab. Her conclusion about bridges is premature.
choices: The additive is unlikely to extend the service life of highway bridges.
Winter salting is the chief cause of cracking in highway bridge decks.
The bacteria closed the cracks in Okafor's damp laboratory samples.
Long-term spore survival is the key question the work leaves unresolved.
explanation: Text 1 reports that the cracked samples sealed, and Text 2 starts by granting it: "Okafor's samples did seal themselves." The two authors split only over what that result means for bridges. The one thing both accept is the laboratory finding, so you look for the claim Text 2 concedes, not the one it attacks.

A.why: You saw that Text 2 rejects Okafor's conclusion and then pushed it too far. Text 2 calls the bridge claim "premature", meaning it hasn't been shown yet. It never says the additive is unlikely to work. Okafor would reject this statement anyway, so it fails twice.

B.why: You picked up a side detail from Text 2's list of bridge conditions. Text 2 mentions salting but never ranks it as a cause of cracking, and Text 1 never mentions it.

D.why: This is Text 2's view, stated correctly, but it isn't Okafor's view. Okafor treats the bridge benefit as settled and doesn't see anything left unresolved. You gave Text 1 an opinion that only Text 2 holds.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Testing cloth scraps from a fourteenth-century Baltic port, historian Liesel Varga detected indigotin, the blue colorant in indigo. The scraps were woven in a pattern typical of the town's own workshops, and Varga therefore argues that local dyers were using indigo imported from India, centuries earlier than such trade is usually dated.

Text 2
Varga's detection is sound. Yet indigotin is also the colorant in woad, a plant widely grown in northern Europe at the time, and her test gives an identical result for either source. Her evidence fits Indian indigo; it does not establish it.
choices: The cloth scraps from the Baltic port contain the colorant indigotin.
The scraps were dyed with locally grown woad rather than Indian indigo.
The scraps were dyed in the town rather than arriving as finished cloth.
Varga's test cannot reveal where the dye in a fabric originated.
explanation: Text 1 reports finding indigotin, and Text 2 accepts it: "Varga's detection is sound." Text 2 disputes only the step from indigotin to Indian indigo, so the shared ground is the chemical finding itself.

B.why: You noticed that Text 2 brings in woad and treated it as Text 2's answer. Text 2 says the test cannot tell the two sources apart ("fits Indian indigo; it does not establish it"). It doesn't claim the dye was woad, and Varga would reject this statement.

C.why: The local weaving pattern is a supporting detail in Text 1. Text 2 never mentions it, so you can't say both authors agree about it.

D.why: This is Text 2's objection, but Varga relies on her test to trace the dye to India. You gave Text 1's author a view that undercuts her own argument.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Twelve distance runners lived at 2,400 meters for four weeks while a matched group stayed at sea level. Back at sea level, the altitude group cut its 5,000-meter times by 1.6 percent; the other group improved by 0.4 percent. The researchers concluded that living at altitude boosts endurance performance.

Text 2
The altitude group's larger gain is not in dispute. But those runners also spent the month at a residential camp with full-time coaches and set meals, while the others trained on their own at home. It is difficult to exclude the camp itself as the cause of the difference.
choices: The camp, not the altitude, produced the altitude group's larger gain.
The two groups trained under comparable conditions during the month.
A 1.6 percent improvement is too small to matter in a 5,000-meter race.
The runners who spent the month at altitude improved more than the others.
explanation: Text 1 reports a 1.6 percent gain against 0.4 percent, and Text 2 says the larger gain "is not in dispute." Text 2 offers a different explanation for the same result. It doesn't deny the result, so the observation is what both authors share.

A.why: You spotted Text 2's alternative cause and treated it as proven. Text 2 says only that the camp is "difficult to exclude" as a cause. That is a possibility, not a finding, and the researchers in Text 1 would reject it.

B.why: Text 2's whole objection is that the groups trained under different conditions, a coached camp against training alone at home. Text 2 would reject this statement.

C.why: Neither text questions whether the size of the gain matters. The disagreement is about what caused it, so this choice takes up a question that neither author raises.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
For twelve weeks, adults in a trial ate only between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. but could eat whatever they liked within that window. They lost an average of 3.1 kilograms. The investigators concluded that limiting the hours of eating, independent of what or how much people eat, promotes weight loss.

Text 2
The participants clearly lost weight. However, their food logs show they also ate about 350 fewer calories a day than before the trial, which alone could account for the loss. Without a comparison group eating the same calories over a longer day, the role of timing itself remains untested.
choices: Eating hours matter for weight only through their effect on calories.
Participants in the trial weighed less at the end than at the start.
The trial isolated the effect of meal timing from that of calories.
Twelve weeks is too short to judge whether the weight loss will last.
explanation: Text 1 reports an average loss of 3.1 kilograms, and Text 2 grants that "the participants clearly lost weight." Text 2 disputes only the claim that timing, separate from calories, caused the loss. The weight loss is the common ground.

A.why: You read Text 2's "could account for" as a firm rule. Text 2 says the role of timing "remains untested", which is different from showing that timing has no effect of its own. The investigators in Text 1 would also reject this statement.

C.why: This is the investigators' assumption, and Text 2 rejects it outright. Text 2 points out that calories fell and no group was matched on calories. This statement belongs to Text 1 only.

D.why: Neither author raises how long the study ran. You brought in a familiar criticism of diet studies in place of the one Text 2 actually makes.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
A survey telescope recorded the star Kestrel-19 dimming by 0.8 percent for three hours every 9.2 days. Because the dips were so regular and so uniform in depth, the team concluded that a planet roughly the size of Neptune orbits the star.

Text 2
The periodic dimming of Kestrel-19 is well documented. Yet the telescope's pixels are wide enough to blend in light from a faint background star, and two distant stars eclipsing each other would produce exactly such regular, uniform dips. Until the star's own wobble is measured, calling the object a planet goes beyond the data.
choices: Kestrel-19's brightness falls by a consistent amount at regular intervals.
The dips come from a pair of background stars that eclipse each other.
The object must be confirmed by measuring the star's wobble.
The telescope's pixel size makes its brightness readings unreliable.
explanation: Text 1 describes a uniform 0.8 percent dip every 9.2 days, and Text 2 calls the periodic dimming "well documented." The two authors disagree only about what causes the dips, so the regular, consistent dimming is the statement both accept.

B.why: You recognized that Text 2 offers another explanation and then treated that explanation as the answer. Text 2 says only that eclipsing background stars "would produce" such dips, so the planet claim goes beyond the data. It does not claim that background stars are the cause.

C.why: This is Text 2's condition, but the team in Text 1 has already concluded the object is a planet without any wobble measurement. You gave Text 1 a requirement that it doesn't accept.

D.why: Text 2 says wide pixels can blend light from two stars, not that the brightness readings are wrong. Text 2 actually trusts the dimming data. You stretched a narrow point into a general one.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
An unsigned woodblock print of a heron shows a hairline white break across the bird's neck, left by a crack in the block. The same break appears in every impression signed by the printmaker Haruno Sei. Art historian Mika Dorn therefore concludes that Haruno pulled the unsigned impression personally.

Text 2
The shared break leaves no doubt that the heron came from Haruno's block. But blocks were routinely sold to publishers, who went on printing from them long after the artist had stopped. The break identifies the block, not the hand that inked it.
choices: The unsigned heron was printed by a publisher who had bought the block.
The crack in the block formed after Haruno stopped printing from it.
Signatures are a poor guide to who pulled a given impression.
The unsigned heron and Haruno's signed prints came from one block.
explanation: Dorn's argument depends on the shared break proving a shared block. Text 2 agrees ("no doubt that the heron came from Haruno's block") and disputes only who did the printing. Both authors accept that the prints came from the same block.

A.why: You saw that Text 2 doubts Haruno printed it and jumped to naming who did. Text 2 says only that publishers could have printed from such blocks, so the break doesn't settle who pulled the print. That shows the question is open. It does not show a publisher made this print.

B.why: The break appears in Haruno's own signed impressions, so the crack was already there while Haruno was printing. Both texts rule this out. You'd need to keep both facts in mind at once to catch it.

C.why: Neither text questions the signatures. Text 2's doubt is about the break as evidence, not about signatures as evidence.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a survey of one town, speakers under thirty pronounced the vowel in words like "boot" farther forward in the mouth than speakers over sixty did, a variant several older residents called "sloppy." Linguist Anouk Petrie concluded that the town's speech is shifting, with the younger variant gradually replacing the older one.

Text 2
Petrie's age gap is real. But speakers often adjust their pronunciation over a lifetime, drifting toward conservative forms in middle age, so such a gap could reappear in every generation while the town's speech stays the same. Only re-recording the same speakers decades later would settle it.
choices: The young speakers will adopt the older vowel as they reach middle age.
In the survey, younger speakers fronted the vowel more than older ones did.
Older residents' disapproval of the new vowel will slow its spread.
Comparing age groups at a single moment cannot reveal a sound change.
explanation: Text 1 reports that younger speakers pronounced the vowel farther forward, and Text 2 opens with "Petrie's age gap is real." Text 2 challenges only what the gap means, so the survey finding is what both authors accept.

A.why: You took Text 2's alternative and stated it as a prediction. Text 2 says only that speakers often shift with age and that the gap "could" recur, then says new recordings would be needed to settle it. Petrie would reject this statement as well.

C.why: The "sloppy" comment is a passing detail in Text 1. Neither text argues that disapproval affects how fast the vowel spreads, and Text 2 never mentions it.

D.why: Petrie's conclusion rests on comparing age groups at a single moment, so she obviously thinks it can reveal change. Text 2 says the comparison is ambiguous, which is weaker than saying it "cannot" reveal change. Neither author holds this view as stated.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
When Harlow raised its minimum wage by 14 percent, economist Dana Reyes tracked restaurant employment there and in neighboring Wexley, which kept the old wage. A year later, restaurant headcount in Harlow had grown as fast as Wexley's. Reyes concluded that the increase did not reduce restaurant employment.

Text 2
Harlow's restaurant headcount did keep pace. Payroll records, however, show that the average worker's weekly hours there fell by 6 percent; restaurants may simply have absorbed the cost by scheduling each worker less. Headcount alone cannot show that the increase left the demand for labor untouched.
choices: Raising a minimum wage reduces employment once hours worked are counted.
Wexley's restaurants were a poor basis for comparison with Harlow's.
Harlow's restaurant headcount grew at about the same rate as Wexley's.
Harlow's restaurants responded to the higher wage by cutting workers' hours.
explanation: Text 1 reports that Harlow's headcount grew as fast as Wexley's, and Text 2 grants that it "did keep pace." Text 2 limits the scope of Reyes's conclusion by pointing to hours instead of headcount. It doesn't dispute the headcount figures, so those are the common ground.

A.why: You followed Text 2 into a general law. Text 2 is about one city's restaurants and says only that headcount "cannot show" demand was unaffected. It doesn't conclude that minimum-wage increases reduce employment in general.

B.why: Neither text faults the Wexley comparison. Text 2 accepts the headcount comparison and objects to what it leaves out.

D.why: Reyes concludes that employment was unaffected, so this is not her view. Even Text 2 only says restaurants "may" have cut hours to absorb the cost. You attributed Text 2's hedged explanation to both authors as a fact.
